title: Attaining Enlightenment in This Very Body (Sokushin jōbutsu gi)
creator: kukai
note: Kūkai's argument that through esoteric practice one can become a Buddha in this present body.
description: In this short treatise Kūkai defends the central claim of Shingon: buddhahood is not reached after countless lifetimes but can be realised 'in this very body'. He explains it through a verse of eight lines, arguing that the six great elements, earth, water, fire, wind, space and consciousness, constitute both the Buddha and all beings and interpenetrate without obstruction; that the four kinds of mandala express this reality; and that the 'three mysteries' of body, speech and mind, practised through mudrā, mantra and meditation, unite the practitioner with Mahāvairocana. With his works on the meanings of sound and of the syllable 'hūṃ', it forms the core of Kūkai's philosophy of language and embodiment.

title: Ten Stages of Mind (Jūjūshinron)
creator: kukai
note: Kūkai's ranking of all known philosophies, from animal appetite to esoteric Buddhism, as ten stages of the mind's development.
description: In 830 Emperor Junna asked the Buddhist schools to submit summaries of their doctrines, and Kūkai responded with the ten-fascicle Himitsu mandara jūjūshinron and its abridgement, the Precious Key to the Secret Treasury (Hizō hōyaku). The ten stages lead from the mind that, like a goat, knows only food and sex, through the ethical mind awakened by Confucianism and the mind seeking heaven, to the Hīnayāna, Yogācāra, Mādhyamaka, Tendai and Kegon schools, and finally to the esoteric mind of Shingon, which contains all the others. Each lower stage is a partial truth rather than an error. The work is both a doctrinal classification in the tradition of Tiantai and Huayan and the first systematic comparative philosophy written in Japan.

title: Teaching, Practice, Faith and Realisation (Kyōgyōshinshō)
creator: shinran
note: Shinran's main work, an anthology of scriptural passages with his commentary establishing salvation through Amida's other power.
description: The six-fascicle Kyōgyōshinshō, properly Ken jōdo shinjitsu kyōgyōshō monrui, was begun, according to the True Pure Land tradition, around 1224 in the Kantō and revised until late in Shinran's life. It assembles passages from sutras and from Indian, Chinese and Japanese masters, with Shinran's interpretations, to show that the true teaching is the Larger Sutra of Immeasurable Life, the true practice is saying Amida's name, the true faith is the entrusting given by Amida, and the true realisation is birth in the Pure Land and nirvana. Shinran rereads classical Chinese passages so that the agent of faith becomes Amida rather than the believer. An autograph manuscript at Higashi Honganji is a National Treasure. It is the foundational text of Jōdo Shinshū, the largest Buddhist denomination in Japan.
image_caption: Manuscript of the Kyōgyōshinshō

title: A Record in Lament of Divergences (Tannishō)
creator: shinran
note: Shinran's sayings recorded by his disciple Yuien, including the claim that if the good are saved, all the more so the wicked.
description: The Tannishō was written about thirty years after Shinran's death, probably by his disciple Yuien, who 'laments' the divergences from his master's teaching that had arisen among followers. Its first part records sayings of Shinran in vivid Japanese, including his declaration that he does not know whether the nembutsu leads to the Pure Land or to hell, and the paradox that if even good people attain birth, how much more the evil person; the second part corrects specific errors. The fifteenth-century Shin leader Rennyo restricted access to it; rediscovered in the Meiji era by Kiyozawa Manshi, it became one of the most read religious texts of modern Japan and attracted philosophers such as Nishida and Tanabe.

title: Universal Recommendation for Zazen (Fukan zazengi)
creator: dogen
note: Dōgen's instructions on seated meditation, written after his return from China; his autograph is a National Treasure.
description: Dōgen composed the Fukan zazengi soon after returning from China in 1227, to make the practice of zazen available to everyone, and revised it in 1233; the autograph of that version, in elegant Chinese, survives at Eihei-ji and is designated a National Treasure. It explains how to sit, breathe and hold the mind, but also insists that zazen is not a method for attaining awakening: it is 'the dharma gate of ease and joy', the practice-realisation of awakening itself. Recited daily in Sōtō temples, it is the shortest statement of the conviction that runs through all of Dōgen's work.
image_caption: Dōgen's autograph of the Fukan zazengi, Tenpuku-era copy of 1233, Eihei-ji

title: Treasury of the True Dharma Eye (Shōbōgenzō)
creator: dogen
note: Dōgen's essays in Japanese on being-time, buddha-nature, practice and language, the major work of Japanese Zen philosophy.
description: The Shōbōgenzō is a collection of essays, many delivered as talks to Dōgen's monks between 1231 and 1253, that survives in compilations of 75, 12 and later 95 chapters. Written in a Japanese dense with Chinese Buddhist terms, puns and deliberate rereadings of classical phrases, it explores 'Genjōkōan', where to study the self is to forget the self; 'Uji' (being-time), which identifies existence with time; 'Busshō' (buddha-nature), which reads the phrase 'all sentient beings have buddha-nature' as 'all beings are buddha-nature' and identifies buddha-nature with impermanence; and topics of monastic practice. Little studied outside Sōtō for centuries, it was rediscovered by Watsuji Tetsurō in the 1920s and is now recognised as one of the summits of Japanese thought, often compared with Heidegger.

title: Treatise on the Three Virtues (Santokushō)
creator: hayashi-razan
note: Hayashi Razan's explanation in Japanese of wisdom, humaneness and courage, popularising Zhu Xi learning.
description: The Santokushō takes its theme from the Doctrine of the Mean, which names wisdom, humaneness and courage as the three universal virtues, and expounds them in simple Japanese for samurai and other readers who could not read Chinese. Hayashi Razan explains Zhu Xi's teaching that the virtues are principle inherent in the mind and that cultivation requires reverent seriousness, and applies it to the hierarchy of Tokugawa society. Works of this kind, alongside his lectures and his role at the shogunate, did much to make Neo-Confucian vocabulary part of Edo culture, though the dating and attribution of some of Razan's Japanese writings are uncertain.

title: Dialogue with an Old Man (Okina mondō)
creator: nakae-toju
note: Nakae Tōju's dialogue in Japanese teaching filial piety as the root of the universe and the way of sagehood for all.
description: In the Okina mondō a disciple questions an old teacher on the meaning of learning and the Way. Nakae Tōju answers that filial piety is not only duty to parents but the virtue that unites a person with heaven, earth and the 'Great Lord on High', the source of all life, and that learning means cultivating the mind rather than reading books. Written in plain Japanese and addressed to warriors, farmers and women alike, it adapts Confucian teaching to circumstances, a point Tōju stressed in the idea of acting according to time, place and status. Printed after his death, it made him one of the best-loved Confucians of Japan and an early exponent of Wang Yangming's learning.

title: The Meaning of Terms in the Analects and Mencius (Gomō jigi)
creator: ito-jinsai
note: Itō Jinsai's redefinition of key Confucian terms from the ancient texts, rejecting Song metaphysics.
description: Jinsai drafted the Gomō jigi in 1683 and revised it throughout his life; it was printed in the year of his death. In thirty entries, on terms such as the Way of heaven, fate, the Way, principle, virtue, humaneness, the mind, nature and loyalty, he argues from the Analects and the Mencius that Song scholars had imported Buddhist and Daoist ideas of quiescence and an abstract principle. For Jinsai the universe is a single living, generative qi; the Way is the path of everyday human relations; and humaneness is love. The book anticipated by a century Dai Zhen's similar project in China, and it set the method of 'ancient learning' (kogaku) in Japan.

title: Boy's Questions (Dōjimon)
creator: ito-jinsai
note: Jinsai's late work in question-and-answer form, explaining the Way of humaneness as love in ordinary life.
description: The Dōjimon presents Jinsai's teaching as a series of questions from a young student and the master's answers, in three fascicles. It returns to his central themes: that the Analects is the supreme book in the universe, that the Way lies in the everyday relations of ruler and subject, parent and child, husband and wife, sibling and friend, and that humaneness is essentially love and lies close at hand. It insists that learning should cultivate practical virtue rather than speculation on human nature. Published two years after his death, it is the most accessible statement of his mature thought.

title: Distinguishing the Way (Bendō)
creator: ogyu-sorai
note: Ogyū Sorai's declaration that the Way is not a natural or moral principle but the rites, music and institutions created by the ancient kings.
description: In the Bendō and its companion Benmei (Distinguishing Names), both completed in 1717, Sorai attacked Song Neo-Confucians and Itō Jinsai alike for misunderstanding the ancient language of the classics. The Way of the sages, he argued, is a collective name for the rites, music, punishments and government that the early kings invented to pacify the realm; it was not found in nature or in the mind but made, and its purpose is the peace and welfare of the people rather than personal cultivation. Individuals contribute by developing their particular talents in service of that order. The work is the key text of Sorai's school and of what Maruyama Masao read as the separation of politics from ethics in Tokugawa thought.

title: Discourse on Government (Seidan)
creator: ogyu-sorai
location: Edo; submitted to the shogun Tokugawa Yoshimune
note: Sorai's confidential proposals to the shogun on reforming samurai life, population registration and the economy.
description: Written privately for the shogun Tokugawa Yoshimune, the Seidan diagnoses the ills of Tokugawa society: samurai living like 'travellers in an inn' in castle towns, dependent on merchants and money, and a population drifting out of control. Sorai proposes returning samurai to the land, strict household registration, sumptuary laws and the reestablishment of institutions in the spirit of the ancient kings. The text circulated in manuscript and was printed only much later. It shows how Sorai's philosophy of the Way as institutions translated into concrete statecraft, and is a key source for Edo social history.

title: Commentary on the Kojiki (Kojiki-den)
creator: motoori-norinaga
note: Norinaga's forty-four-volume decipherment of the Kojiki, which recovered how Japan's oldest chronicle was to be read in Japanese.
description: The Kojiki, compiled in 712, records Japan's myths and early imperial history in a mixture of Chinese characters used for meaning and sound that had become almost unreadable. Motoori Norinaga spent thirty-five years reconstructing its readings in ancient Japanese, word by word, and commenting on every passage. In the introductory essay Naobi no mitama he argued that the Kojiki records the true Way of the gods, received from the sun goddess Amaterasu, which needs no Chinese moralising and can only be accepted, not rationalised. The philology was a monumental scholarly achievement still used today; the theology made the Kojiki a central text of later Shinto nationalism.
image_caption: Printed volume of the Kojiki-den

title: The Essentials of the Tale of Genji (Shibun yōryō)
creator: motoori-norinaga
note: Norinaga's argument that the Tale of Genji should be read not as moral instruction but as an expression of mono no aware.
description: In 1763 Norinaga wrote two treatises, the Shibun yōryō on The Tale of Genji and the Isonokami sasamegoto on poetry. Rejecting Buddhist and Confucian readings of Genji as a moral allegory or warning against lust, he argued that the novel's purpose is to make readers know mono no aware, the capacity to be deeply moved by things, and that its characters are judged good or bad by their sensitivity, not by conventional morality. This theory of literature as the expression and cultivation of feeling became one of the cornerstones of Japanese aesthetics and of Norinaga's wider critique of Chinese rationalism.

title: The Way of Nature and Labour (Shizen shin'eidō)
creator: ando-shoeki
location: Hachinohe, Mutsu; manuscript mostly lost in 1923
note: Andō Shōeki's attack on all rulers, sages and priests as parasites on farmers, and his vision of an egalitarian 'world of nature'.
description: The Shizen shin'eidō survives in a three-fascicle printed version of 1753 and fragments of a manuscript of about a hundred fascicles, most of which was destroyed in the fire after the 1923 earthquake. Shōeki describes nature as a self-moving process of advancing and retreating qi, in which men and women, heaven and earth, form complementary pairs without hierarchy. In the original 'world of nature' everyone farmed; then sages, Buddhas and rulers created the 'world of law', with its classes and doctrines, in order to eat without working. He prescribes 'direct cultivation' by all. Unknown until 1899, the work has been read as a precursor of anarchism and ecological thought.
image_caption: Page of Andō Shōeki's Shizen shin'eidō

title: An Encouragement of Learning (Gakumon no susume)
creator: fukuzawa-yukichi
note: Seventeen pamphlets urging practical learning as the basis of personal and national independence; one of the bestsellers of Meiji Japan.
description: Fukuzawa Yukichi's series opens with the famous statement that, it is said, heaven does not create one person above or below another, and argues that differences in status come from learning. By learning he meant practical knowledge, reading, writing, arithmetic, geography, physics, economics and ethics, which enables people to stand on their own and so to build an independent nation. Later pamphlets discuss the equality of nations, the duties of citizens, the evils of servility and the role of private initiative. Written in plain Japanese, the series sold, by Fukuzawa's estimate, over three million copies, about one for every ten Japanese, and shaped the values of Meiji education.
image_caption: Early edition of Gakumon no susume

title: An Outline of a Theory of Civilization (Bunmeiron no gairyaku)
creator: fukuzawa-yukichi
note: Fukuzawa's argument, drawing on Guizot and Buckle, that civilisation is the advance of a people's knowledge and virtue, and that Japan must pursue it to stay independent.
description: Fukuzawa's most systematic work describes civilisation as a relative and progressive state, measured by the knowledge and virtue of the whole people rather than by its rulers. Drawing on the historians François Guizot and Henry Thomas Buckle, he argued that Western nations were 'civilised', China and Japan 'half-civilised', and that Japan's traditional imbalance of power, which concentrated authority in the government, had stunted the people's spirit. The goal of civilisation in Japan's present situation, he concluded, was the preservation of national independence. The book is the classic of the Meiji enlightenment and was re-examined in detail by Maruyama Masao.
image_caption: Title page of the first edition of Bunmeiron no gairyaku, 1875

title: An Inquiry into the Good (Zen no kenkyū)
creator: nishida-kitaro
note: Nishida Kitarō's first book, which built a philosophy of reality, ethics and religion on 'pure experience' prior to subject and object.
description: Written while Nishida was teaching in Kanazawa and published in 1911, An Inquiry into the Good begins from pure experience, the direct awareness of, for example, a colour or a sound before one judges that 'I' perceive 'it'. From there Nishida argues that reality is a single self-developing system of consciousness, that the good is the realisation of the self's true personality in unity with that reality, and that religion is the deepest form of this unity, which he linked to God. He drew on William James, Wundt, Hegel and his own Zen practice. Often called the first original work of modern Japanese philosophy, it was widely read by students and remains Nishida's most accessible book.

title: Climate and Culture (Fūdo)
creator: watsuji-tetsuro
note: Watsuji's study of how climate and landscape shape human existence, in monsoon, desert and meadow cultures.
description: Fūdo grew out of Watsuji's sea voyage to Europe in 1927 and his reading of Heidegger's Being and Time, which he felt neglected the spatial and social dimension of existence. Human beings, he argued, discover themselves through fūdo, the climate and environment in which they live; the cold we feel is not merely a physical state but a way in which we already exist together outside ourselves. He distinguishes three types: the monsoon of South and East Asia, receptive and resigned; the desert, combative and submissive to a single god; and the European meadow, regular and rational, with a special analysis of Japan. The typology has been criticised as essentialist, but the book founded a philosophy of environment and is still widely read.

title: Ethics (Rinrigaku)
creator: watsuji-tetsuro
note: Watsuji's three-volume system of ethics as the study of ningen, human beings in their 'betweenness'.
description: Watsuji built his ethics on the Japanese word ningen, written with characters meaning 'person' and 'between', to argue that a human being is at once an individual and a member of relationships, and that ethics is the study of the 'betweenness' (aidagara) in which we exist. Individuality arises by negating the community and the community by negating the individual, in a continuing double negation that ultimately expresses emptiness. The volumes trace this structure through family, kin, local community, economy, culture and the state. Its account of the state was criticised after the war and revised by Watsuji; the work is the most systematic ethical philosophy of modern Japan.

title: Philosophy as Metanoetics (Zangedō to shite no tetsugaku)
creator: tanabe-hajime
note: Tanabe's confession that reason had failed in the war, and his call for a philosophy that passes through repentance and other power.
description: Tanabe delivered the substance of this book as lectures in the autumn of 1944, as Japan's defeat loomed, and published it in 1946. Feeling that he had neither resisted nor rightly guided his nation, he concluded that philosophy itself must undergo zange, repentance or metanoia: reason must recognise its own powerlessness and surrender to an 'other power' that restores it in a new form. Drawing on Shinran's Pure Land faith and on Kant, Hegel and Kierkegaard, he called this 'metanoetics', a philosophy that is not his own work but the action of absolute nothingness through him. The book is a rare example of a philosopher's public self-criticism after the war.

title: Religion and Nothingness (Shūkyō to wa nanika)
creator: nishitani-keiji
note: Nishitani's analysis of modern nihilism and his account of the 'field of emptiness' in which things appear as they are.
description: The essays collected as Shūkyō to wa nanika ('What is religion?') ask how religion is possible after science and Nietzsche. Nishitani argues that the modern self, which treats everything as an object of its own representation, is underlain by a 'field of nihility' revealed in anxiety and the sense of meaninglessness. Rather than fleeing it, one must pass through it to the 'field of emptiness' (śūnyatā), where self and things are no longer opposed and each appears in its own mode of being, in a circuminsession with all others. He engages Christianity, Eckhart, Nietzsche and Heidegger, as well as Zen. Translated by Jan Van Bragt in 1982, it is the most influential Kyoto School book in the West.

title: Place (Basho)
creator: nishida-kitaro
location: Tokyo: in the journal Tetsugaku kenkyū
note: The essay in which Nishida introduced his 'logic of place', locating all beings ultimately in absolute nothingness.
description: Published in 1926 and later included in From the Acting to the Seeing, 'Basho' turned Nishida from the psychology of experience to logic. Aristotle had defined substance as what is a subject and never a predicate; Nishida reverses the perspective and asks about the 'place' in which subjects and predicates, knower and known, are located. Physical things are located in a field of consciousness, which is in turn located in deeper places, until one reaches a place of 'absolute nothingness' that cannot itself be objectified. This logic of basho became the core of Nishida's mature philosophy and the defining idea of the Kyoto School.

title: Commentary on the Awakening of Faith (Daeseung gisillon so)
creator: wonhyo
note: Wonhyo's commentary on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna, which reads the 'one mind' as reconciling the schools; studied in China and Japan.
description: The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna, a sixth-century treatise probably composed in China, teaches that one mind has two aspects, suchness and arising-and-ceasing, and so unites the doctrines of buddha-nature and of the storehouse consciousness. Wonhyo wrote two commentaries on it, the Gisillon so and the Byeolgi, arguing that the text resolves the conflict between Madhyamaka emptiness and Yogācāra analysis, which are like the two sides of one coin. Fazang drew on Wonhyo's work in his own celebrated commentary, and Wonhyo's was among the 'three great commentaries' on the treatise in East Asia. It is the clearest statement of the one-mind philosophy that underlies his whole work.

title: Ten Approaches to the Reconciliation of Doctrinal Controversy (Simmun hwajaeng non)
creator: wonhyo
note: Wonhyo's treatise showing that apparently opposed Buddhist doctrines are partial perspectives on one truth.
description: In this treatise, now surviving only in fragments discovered on woodblocks at Haeinsa, Wonhyo took up ten disputed questions of his time, such as whether all beings possess buddha-nature, whether emptiness and existence conflict, and whether the self and the dharmas are real, and showed that each side was correct from its own standpoint and mistaken only in denying the other. The method of hwajaeng, harmonising disputes, made his work a touchstone for later Korean Buddhists, and modern scholars have taken it as the distinctive character of Korean Buddhism, though how far it differs from Chinese doctrinal classification is debated.

title: Exposition of the Vajrasamādhi Sutra (Geumgang sammaegyeong non)
creator: wonhyo
note: Wonhyo's late commentary on an apocryphal sutra possibly composed in Silla, a synthesis of Seon, Yogācāra and one-mind teaching.
description: The Vajrasamādhi Sutra was probably composed in East Asia in the seventh century, and some scholars argue it was written in Silla itself. According to Wonhyo's biography in the Song Biographies of Eminent Monks, a dragon king gave the sutra to the Silla court and only Wonhyo could explain it; he lectured on it riding on an ox, writing his commentary between its horns. Uniquely for a commentary, it was given the title non, 'treatise', normally reserved for works by bodhisattvas. Wonhyo uses the sutra to integrate meditation with doctrine around the theme of the 'contemplation practice of a single taste'. It is often considered his most mature work.

title: Diagram of the Dharma Realm of the One Vehicle of Hwaeom (Hwaeom ilseung beopgye do)
creator: uisang
location: Tang China (Zhixiang monastery, Mount Zhongnan); presented to Zhiyan
note: A 210-character poem arranged as a winding path in a square seal, condensing the Huayan vision that one is all and all is one.
description: Uisang composed this work in 668 while studying with Zhiyan in China and presented it to his teacher shortly before Zhiyan's death. It is a poem of thirty lines of seven characters, arranged on a single red line that winds through a square grid in fifty-four turns, beginning and ending at the centre with the character for dharma and the character for Buddha. Its verses state that the dharma-nature is perfectly interfused, that one is in all and all is in one, and that a single mote of dust contains the ten directions. Uisang added an explanatory commentary. Recited and copied in Korean monasteries ever since, the diagram is the founding document of Korean Hwaeom and a striking union of poetry, image and philosophy.

title: Secrets on Cultivating the Mind (Susim gyeol)
creator: jinul
note: Jinul's concise guide to sudden awakening and gradual cultivation, the most widely read work of Korean Seon.
description: Written in the form of questions and answers, the Susim gyeol explains that the mind of every person is Buddha and that one must look within rather than seek outside. Awakening to this is sudden, like realising one's mistake on waking; but long-accumulated habits remain, so it must be followed by gradual cultivation, as ice that is water by nature still needs time to melt. Jinul describes this cultivation as the balanced practice of samādhi and prajñā, and answers objections from those who think practice unnecessary after awakening. It remains a standard text for Korean monks and lay practitioners and was translated by Robert Buswell.

title: Excerpts from the Dharma Collection with Personal Notes (Beopjip byeolhaeng nok jeoryo byeongip sagi)
creator: jinul
note: Jinul's final work, a critical summary of Zongmi's account of the Chan schools, culminating in the use of the hwadu.
description: In this major treatise Jinul quotes and comments on the Chinese master Zongmi's comparison of the Chan lineages, accepting his argument that understanding must precede practice and that awakening is sudden while cultivation is gradual. He then goes beyond Zongmi, concluding with Dahui's 'shortcut' method of investigating a hwadu, a critical phrase from a Chan dialogue, as the means to cut through conceptual understanding. The work became part of the Korean monastic curriculum and fixed the Korean Seon synthesis of doctrinal study, gradual cultivation and kanhwa meditation.

title: Array of Critiques of Buddhism (Bulssi japbyeon)
creator: jeong-dojeon
note: Jeong Do-jeon's systematic Neo-Confucian refutation of Buddhist doctrines, written in the last year of his life.
description: In nineteen short chapters Jeong Do-jeon attacks the Buddhist teachings of transmigration, karma, the mind as source of all things, the illusoriness of the world, and the renunciation of family life, using the Cheng-Zhu philosophy of principle and material force: the dispersal of qi at death disproves rebirth; the Buddhists see the mind but not the principle within it; and their withdrawal from human relations destroys the moral order. He also blames the decline of past dynasties on Buddhist patronage. Completed in 1398, the year of his murder, it was published in 1456 and provided the intellectual basis for the Joseon state's long suppression of Buddhism.

title: Ten Diagrams on Sage Learning (Seonghak sipdo)
creator: yi-hwang
note: Toegye's ten diagrams with commentary summarising Neo-Confucian cosmology, ethics and self-cultivation for the young king.
description: In 1568, at the age of sixty-eight, Yi Hwang presented ten diagrams to the seventeen-year-old King Seonjo, so that the king might keep them before him as a screen or album. Seven derive from earlier Chinese and Korean scholars, among them Zhou Dunyi's diagram of the Supreme Ultimate and the Western Inscription, and three are Toegye's own; each is accompanied by a text and his commentary. They lead from the cosmos through the Great Learning and elementary learning to the relation of mind, nature and feelings, the Four-Seven question and the practice of reverence in daily life. Compact and profound, it is the best-known summary of Korean Neo-Confucianism and was frequently printed in Korea and Japan.

title: Four–Seven Debate Letters (Sadan chiljeong non)
creator: yi-hwang
location: Andong and Hanyang; letters between Yi Hwang and Gi Dae-seung
note: The letters in which Toegye and the young scholar Gi Dae-seung argued over whether the four moral feelings and seven emotions arise from principle or from material force.
description: In 1559 Gi Dae-seung (Gobong), twenty-six years Toegye's junior, questioned a formulation in which Yi Hwang had said that the four beginnings of Mencius (compassion, shame, deference and the sense of right) issue from principle and the seven emotions of the Book of Rites from material force. Gi argued that the four are simply the good portion of the seven and that principle and qi cannot be separated. Over seven years of respectful letters Toegye refined his view: in the four, principle issues and qi follows; in the seven, qi issues and principle rides on it. The exchange, later continued by Yi I and Seong Hon, raised questions about the relation of moral and ordinary emotion that Chinese Neo-Confucians had left untouched, and it defined Korean philosophy for three centuries.

title: Essentials of the Studies of the Sages (Seonghak jibyo)
creator: yi-i
note: Yulgok's reorganisation of Neo-Confucian learning as a guide for the ruler, from self-cultivation to governing the state.
description: Yi I presented the Seonghak jibyo to King Seonjo in 1575 as a more practical and Korean alternative to the Chinese Extended Meaning of the Great Learning by Zhen Dexiu. In five parts, following the structure of the Great Learning, it gathers passages from the classics and the Song masters with Yulgok's commentary, moving from the ruler's self-cultivation, through the regulation of his family, to governing and the transmission of the Way. It reflects Yulgok's conviction that moral learning must issue in institutional reform, and became a standard text in the education of later Joseon kings.

title: Essential Secrets for Removing Ignorance (Gyeongmong yogyeol)
creator: yi-i
note: Yulgok's short primer for beginning students on setting one's will, reading the classics and conducting family life.
description: Written in 1577 while Yi I was living in Haeju, the Gyeongmong yogyeol was intended for young students who had just begun to learn. In ten chapters it urges them to set their will on becoming sages, to change old habits, to keep their bodies and minds in order, to read the classics in a prescribed sequence, and to serve their parents, conduct funerals and sacrifices, manage the household and deal with others correctly. Simple and practical, it became one of the most widely used primers in Joseon schools, alongside the Elementary Learning. An autograph manuscript with an inkstone associated with Yulgok is preserved at Ojukheon in Gangneung.

title: Letters to Seong Hon on Principle and Material Force
creator: yi-i
note: Yulgok's exchange with his friend Seong Hon, renewing the Four–Seven debate and arguing that only qi issues and principle rides on it.
description: In 1572 Seong Hon (Ugye) wrote to his friend Yi I asking whether Toegye's view of the four beginnings and seven emotions was correct. In nine replies Yulgok argued that there is only one way in which feelings arise: material force issues and principle rides upon it. The four beginnings are not a separate source but the good part of the seven emotions; principle is universal and pervasive, while qi is particular and limiting, a formula (igi tong guk) that summed up his philosophy. The letters founded the Giho school of Yulgok's followers, which debated Toegye's Yeongnam school for the rest of the Joseon dynasty.

title: Admonitions on Governing the People (Mongmin simseo)
creator: jeong-yak-yong
note: Dasan's forty-eight-chapter handbook for district magistrates on just and humane administration.
description: Written at the end of Jeong Yak-yong's eighteen years of exile in Gangjin, the Mongmin simseo is addressed to the local magistrates who directly governed the Korean people. Its twelve parts, from taking up office to leaving it, cover personal integrity, care for the elderly and destitute, taxes, corvée, justice, rites, the military, public works and famine relief, drawing on Chinese and Korean precedent and on Dasan's own observations of abuses by clerks and officials. Its title calls it the 'heart's book' because the exiled author could only write what he could not carry out. It became a classic of Korean public administration and is still read by officials today.

title: Design for Good Government (Gyeongse yupyo)
creator: jeong-yak-yong
note: Dasan's unfinished blueprint for the reform of the Joseon state, its offices, land system and taxation.
description: Originally titled 'Bangnye chobon', the Gyeongse yupyo uses the Rites of Zhou as a model for the complete reorganisation of the Joseon government: the structure of ministries, the examination and appointment of officials, a well-field land system adapted to Korean conditions, fair taxation and military reform. Jeong Yak-yong left it unfinished but it is the most ambitious institutional plan of the Silhak movement. With the Mongmin simseo on local government and the Heumheum sinseo on criminal justice, it forms the trilogy of Dasan's practical writings.

title: Jehol Diary (Yeolha ilgi)
creator: bak-ji-won
location: Written after the 1780 embassy to Beijing and Jehol
note: Bak Ji-won's account of a journey to Qing China, full of observations on technology and commerce and satires of Joseon society.
description: In 1780 Bak Ji-won travelled with a Joseon embassy to congratulate the Qianlong Emperor on his seventieth birthday, going to Beijing and then to the summer palace at Jehol (Rehe, now Chengde). His account, written in a lively, unorthodox classical style, describes Chinese carts, kilns, bricks, markets and buildings, conversations with Chinese scholars and Tibetan lamas, and argues that Korea should learn from the Qing rather than despising them as barbarians. It also contains the satirical tales 'Master Heo' and 'The Tiger's Rebuke'. Its style was condemned by King Jeongjo, but the book became the classic of the Northern Learning school and of Korean travel writing.
image_caption: Manuscript copy of the Yeolha ilgi

title: Great Scripture of Eastern Learning (Donggyeong daejeon)
creator: choe-je-u
location: Gyeongju; compiled and printed by Choe Si-hyeong
note: Choe Je-u's writings on the Lord of Heaven within each person, the foundation of Donghak and Cheondogyo.
description: The Donggyeong daejeon gathers the essays Choe Je-u wrote in classical Chinese between his revelation of 1860 and his arrest, among them 'Discussion of Learning' (Nonhak mun), which explains why his teaching is 'Eastern Learning' rather than Western Learning, and the twenty-one-character incantation. Its central idea is sicheonju, 'bearing the Lord of Heaven within', which implied the equal dignity of every person irrespective of class. His successor Choe Si-hyeong compiled and printed it in 1880, together with the vernacular songs of the Yongdam yusa. It is the scripture of Donghak and a key text of nineteenth-century Korean thought.

title: On the Reform of Korean Buddhism (Joseon bulgyo yusin non)
creator: han-yong-un
note: Han Yong-un's manifesto for a modern Korean Buddhism grounded in equality, education and engagement with society.
description: Written in 1910 and published in 1913, the treatise argues that Buddhism's core values are equality and saving all beings, which accord with modern ideas of freedom and progress, but that Korean Buddhism had decayed in remote mountain monasteries under centuries of Joseon repression. Han calls for modern education of monks, simplified rituals, the relocation of temples to cities, the abolition of superstitious practices, economic self-reliance and, controversially, permission for monks to marry. Influenced by Liang Qichao's writings and by Japanese Buddhist modernisation, it is the founding document of modern Korean Buddhist reform.
